results.summary: The Reactive Plasma CMOS Inverter is an educational hardware visualizer that generates a 640x480 VGA signal to illustrate the operation of a CMOS NOT gate. It displays a transistor-level schematic, a live oscilloscope waveform, and an active truth table, all driven by an internal frame counter. The design also produces a PWM audio tone that changes pitch with the input state. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock and a VGA monitor, with optional audio output, and is notable for being a demoscene entry that visualizes fundamental CMOS behavior entirely in logic gates.

This project is an analog Low Dropout Regulator designed in the SkyWater 130 nm process, targeting a 1.3 V output from a 1.5 V input with load currents up to 10 mA. It includes a current generator, error amplifier, push-pull composite power transistor, feedback network, and load circuit. Extensive pre-layout simulation results are provided for quiescent current, dropout voltage, load and line regulation, startup, transient response, PSRR, and open-loop gain. The design is notable for its detailed analog documentation and supply-independent current circuit, but silicon validation would require external test equipment such as a DC power supply, electronic load, and oscilloscope.

NeuroPulse is a 4-neuron spiking neural network accelerator using the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model, with weights held off-chip by an RP2040 and streamed via PIO. The FSM processes one neuron at a time in 7 states, achieving about 1.78 million network passes per second at 50 MHz. It supports external spike injection and Hebbian learning (LTP only), with spike outputs and control signals on the pins. The design is notable for its minimal transistor budget (under 2000T) and requires an RP2040 for weight storage and learning updates.

This project implements an 8-bit R-2R ladder DAC intended for Ground Penetrating Radar applications, converting digital signals to analog for antenna transmission. It includes a sine waveform driver and provides a 3.3V output. The DAC can be tested in external data mode by applying digital inputs and observing the analog output, or in internal sawtooth mode. External hardware such as an FPGA board is needed to drive the digital inputs, and the documentation is relatively brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.

DemosceneTTSKY is a fully autonomous VGA visual synthesizer that generates 640x480 video and bytebeat audio entirely from logic gates, with no RAM, ROM, or CPU. It uses an LFSR to randomly change visual equations, shift amounts, and palettes every second, creating evolving fractal patterns. The audio is output on bidirectional pins during video blanking intervals. The design requires a 25 MHz clock and external hardware such as a VGA monitor and a resistor DAC for RGB, plus an optional audio amplifier, and is notable for its self-directing demoscene nature.

The DDS Sine Chirp Beacon is a direct digital synthesis sine source with fixed-tone, chirp, and dual-tone modes, providing an 8-bit parallel sample and a 1-bit PDM output. It uses a 24-bit phase accumulator and a 64-entry sine lookup table, with chirp modes that sweep the frequency over time. The design can be used to excite resonant systems or scan audio paths. External hardware such as an R-2R DAC, RC low-pass filter, and piezo buzzer or amplifier is required to use the outputs, and the documentation is clear about its operation.

DKTT01 - VGA Glider is a modified version of the VGA playground 'Rings' demo, where multi-colored rings move diagonally from the bottom left to the top right corner. It generates a 640x480 VGA signal and is intended to be tested using the TinyTapeout VGA playground guide. No external hardware is required beyond a VGA monitor. The documentation is very brief, providing only a one-line description and basic testing instructions.

Missile Command is a tiny version of Atari's classic game, implemented in Verilog for Tiny Tapeout. It uses a VGA PMOD for video and a GamePad PMOD for control, supporting a single player. The game features missiles, bombs, explosions, a fortress, and level progression, with sprites generated by formulas or predefined matrices. It requires external hardware including a TinyTapeout dev kit, VGA PMOD, GamePad PMOD, monitor, and SNES controller, and is notable for being a complete game implementation on a 2x2 tile footprint.

This project is an analog tile created for the ECE298A course, intended to demonstrate an analog workflow. The documentation is essentially incomplete, stating only that it will be completed later and that built-in self-test is used extensively. No functional description or testing details are provided, and no external hardware is required at the moment. Due to the lack of documentation, it is not possible to determine the specific function or capabilities of the design.

The VGA Clock Demo is a Verilog design that renders a circular analog clock face on a 640x480 VGA display, with background colors and sun/moon positions changing based on the time of day. It includes hour, minute, and second hands, and allows time adjustment via a Gamepad PMOD. The clock starts at 00:00:00 and can be set using the gamepad buttons. It requires a VGA monitor and a Gamepad PMOD, and is notable for its visual representation of time with day/night themes.
